title: Composite and Decorator
scopeHtml: Scope: Composite trees, Decorator stacks, before/after refactors, when not to use, ViewGroup and Java IO examples, comparison.

notes.title: Composite: the idea
notes.html:
Composite lets you treat a single object and a group of objects through the same interface. It models a tree where leaves and containers both answer the same calls, so the client does not care which one it holds.

Mechanism: a Component interface; Leaf implements it directly; Composite implements it by holding a list of Components and forwarding the call to each child (recursion).

+-----------------+
| <<Component>>   |<-----------------------------+
| + size(): long  |                              |
+--------+--------+                              | children
         ^                                       |
   +-----+-----------+                    +------+------+
   |                 |                    |  Folder     |
+--+----+            +------------------->| + add(c)    |
| File  |            implements           | + size()=sum|
| size  |                                 +-------------+
+-------+

Worked example. root holds b.txt (4 KB) and docs. docs holds a.txt (10 KB) and c.pdf (86 KB). root.size() = 4 + (10 + 86) = 100 KB. The client wrote one line, root.size(); the tree did the recursion.

Industry examples. Android View and ViewGroup: a LinearLayout is a View containing Views; measure() and draw() recurse. Compose's UI node tree. The file system. The DOM (Node). Swing's Container/Component. An org chart where salary() of a manager includes the team.

Everyday analogy. A box that can hold items or other boxes. Asking "what is the total weight" works the same for a single item or a box of boxes.

Decision gravity. Adopting it is cheap and reversible while the tree is small. The risky choice is the API: put add() on the Component (uniform, but leaves must throw) or only on the Composite (safe, but clients need casts). Changing that later breaks callers.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the key point: the client treats leaf and composite uniformly.
  • Not handling cycles (a folder added inside itself) which causes infinite recursion.

notes.title: Composite in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before. The client must know the types and loop itself.

// BEFORE: caller branches on type and recurses by hand
long total(Object node) {
    if (node instanceof File f) return f.size;
    long sum = 0;
    for (Object c : ((Folder) node).children) sum += total(c);
    return sum;
}

After.

import java.util.*;

interface FsNode { long size(); }

class FileNode implements FsNode {
    private final long kb;
    FileNode(long kb) { this.kb = kb; }
    public long size() { return kb; }
}

class FolderNode implements FsNode {
    private final List<FsNode> children = new ArrayList<>();
    FolderNode add(FsNode n) { children.add(n); return this; }
    public long size() {
        long sum = 0;
        for (FsNode c : children) sum += c.size();
        return sum;
    }
}

// new FolderNode().add(new FileNode(4))
//     .add(new FolderNode().add(new FileNode(10)).add(new FileNode(86))).size() == 100
sealed interface FsNode { fun size(): Long }
class FileNode(private val kb: Long) : FsNode { override fun size() = kb }
class FolderNode(private val children: MutableList<FsNode> = mutableListOf()) : FsNode {
    fun add(n: FsNode) = apply { children += n }
    override fun size() = children.sumOf { it.size() }
}

Safety vs transparency. Transparent composite: add/remove in the interface, leaves throw UnsupportedOperationException. Safe composite: add/remove only in the folder class. Interviewers like you to name both trade-offs.

Common interview traps.

  • Deep recursion on very deep trees causes StackOverflowError; mention iterative traversal with an explicit stack.
  • Caching size() in a parent without invalidating when a child changes.

notes.title: Composite: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not use it when the structure is not truly a tree (graphs with shared nodes and cycles need different handling) or when leaves and containers have very different operations. Forcing a shared interface makes half the methods meaningless.

Do not use it for a flat list of two or three items; a plain List is clearer.

Watch the cost: operations touch every node. size() on a million-file tree is O(n) unless cached; real file systems keep directory totals out of band.

Worked example. A UI toolkit gave every widget addChild(). Button.addChild() threw. That produced a crash in 1 out of ~200 QA scenarios. The fix was a separate Container type holding children.

Common interview traps.

  • Asserting Composite fits all hierarchies. It fits part-whole trees where uniform treatment matters.
  • Ignoring the O(n) cost of recursion on huge trees.

notes.title: Decorator: the idea
notes.html:
Decorator adds behavior to an object at runtime by wrapping it in another object with the same interface. You stack wrappers like layers, each doing a little extra before or after delegating to the thing inside.

Mechanism: the decorator implements the same interface as the thing it wraps and holds it. Its method does extra work, then (or before) calls inner.method().

+---------------+
| <<DataSource>>|<--------------------------+
| read()        |                           |
+-------+-------+                           | wraps (has-a)
        ^                           +-------+--------+
   +----+---------+                 | Decorator      |
   | FileSource   |                 | inner          |
   +--------------+                 +---+--------+---+
                                        ^        ^
                                 Buffered     Compressed

Worked example. Reading a log file: FileSource returns 1 byte per call. Wrapping it in Buffering (8 KB buffer) turns 8,192 disk calls into 1. Adding Compression makes a 100 MB file read as 12 MB from disk. You composed 3 behaviors without a BufferedCompressedEncryptedFileSource class.

Industry examples. Java IO: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f))). Collections.unmodifiableList(list) and Collections.synchronizedList(list). Android ContextWrapper (ancestor of Activity) wraps a Context. OkHttp's GzipSource/BufferedSource layers. Kotlin by delegation is built for this.

Everyday analogy. Ordering coffee: espresso, then add milk, then add caramel. Each add-on wraps the previous drink and changes the price and description.

Decision gravity. Reversible and cheap for small stacks. The one-way risk is exposing it in a public API where callers depend on layer ORDER (compress-then-encrypt is not the same as encrypt-then-compress: encrypted data does not compress).

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up Decorator with inheritance: decorator is runtime composition, inheritance is compile-time.
  • Forgetting that wrapper order changes behavior.

notes.title: Decorator in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before. Subclass explosion for every combination.

// BEFORE: a class per feature combination
class BufferedFileReader {}
class EncryptedFileReader {}
class BufferedEncryptedFileReader {}
class BufferedEncryptedCompressedFileReader {} // 2^n classes

After.

interface Source { String read(); }

class FileSource implements Source {
    public String read() { return "hello world"; }
}

abstract class SourceDecorator implements Source {
    protected final Source inner;
    SourceDecorator(Source inner) { this.inner = inner; }
}

class UpperCase extends SourceDecorator {
    UpperCase(Source s) { super(s); }
    public String read() { return inner.read().toUpperCase(); }
}

class Timed extends SourceDecorator {
    Timed(Source s) { super(s); }
    public String read() {
        long t = System.nanoTime();
        String r = inner.read();
        System.out.println("read took " + (System.nanoTime() - t) / 1000 + " us");
        return r;
    }
}

// new Timed(new UpperCase(new FileSource())).read()  -> "HELLO WORLD", plus timing
interface Source { fun read(): String }
class FileSource : Source { override fun read() = "hello world" }

// 'by inner' forwards every method; we override only what we change
class UpperCase(private val inner: Source) : Source by inner {
    override fun read() = inner.read().uppercase()
}
class Timed(private val inner: Source) : Source by inner {
    override fun read(): String {
        val t = System.nanoTime()
        return inner.read().also { println("took ${(System.nanoTime() - t) / 1000} us") }
    }
}
// Timed(UpperCase(FileSource())).read()

Common interview traps.

  • Decorator must implement the SAME interface; if it adds new methods, callers holding the base type cannot reach them.
  • Identity checks (==, instanceof) break because the wrapper is a different object.
  • Large interfaces make decorators verbose in Java; Kotlin by fixes that.

notes.title: Decorator: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not use it when the base interface is huge (every decorator must forward 30 methods in Java) or when callers need the concrete type (casting through layers is fragile).

Skip it when the combination of features is fixed: a plain class is simpler and faster to debug. Deep stacks hurt debuggability: a stack trace 12 frames deep through wrappers, and per-call overhead.

If you only need behavior around one method (logging, auth), a Filter/Interceptor chain or AOP may be a better fit than hand-built wrappers.

Worked example. A team stacked 9 wrappers around HttpClient. A bug where retry wrapped logging twice doubled log volume (2x of 40 GB/day = extra 40 GB). Reordering wrappers was the fix, and no test pinned the order.

Common interview traps.

  • Offering Decorator when a simple subclass or a config flag does the job.
  • Not testing wrapper ORDER.

notes.title: Decorator vs Composite vs inheritance
notes.html:
All three are about structure, but they answer different questions.

Composite Decorator Inheritance
Shape One object holds MANY children One wrapper holds ONE inner Parent/child class
Goal Uniform part-whole tree Add behavior at runtime Reuse + specialize at compile time
Changes at runtime Yes (add/remove children) Yes (stack/unstack) No
Example ViewGroup, folders BufferedReader class Dog extends Animal

Both Composite and Decorator rely on the same trick: the wrapper has the same interface as what it holds. A Decorator is like a Composite with exactly one child whose purpose is to add behavior, not to aggregate.

Industry examples. Android View tree = Composite. ContextThemeWrapper = Decorator. A Java IO pipeline uses Decorator; the file tree it reads is Composite.

Everyday analogy. Composite is a team (many people, treated as "the team"). Decorator is a person putting on a coat, hat, then gloves (each layer adds something).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing "has many" with "wraps one".
  • Replying "Decorator is just inheritance"; the key is runtime and stackable.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Composite: one interface for leaf and group; recursion does the work; model part-whole trees (ViewGroup, file systems, DOM).
  • Choose transparent (add on interface) or safe (add on folder) knowingly; guard against cycles and deep recursion.
  • Decorator: same interface wrapper that adds behavior at runtime; stackable; order matters (BufferedReader, unmodifiableList, ContextWrapper).
  • Kotlin by delegation removes the forwarding boilerplate.
  • Avoid Decorator for huge interfaces or fixed feature sets; avoid Composite when it is not a real tree.
  • Composite = many children; Decorator = exactly one inner and extra behavior.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Composite pattern? Explain with a file system and with Android views.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you see "treat one and many the same" and know the recursion lives in the container.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Composite lets a client treat a single object and a group of objects through one interface. A File is a leaf, a Folder holds a list of the same interface type, and size() on a folder sums its children, recursively. Android's View is the component, ViewGroup the composite: measure() and draw() recurse down the tree.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three roles: Component (interface), Leaf (does the work), Composite (holds List<Component> and forwards the call). The client calls root.size() and never checks types.

Folder root -> File b.txt (4)
            -> Folder docs -> File a.txt (10), File c.pdf (86)
root.size() = 4 + (10 + 86) = 100

Other examples: DOM Node, Swing Container, an org chart where a manager's salary() includes the team. It is for part-whole trees only.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface FsNode { long size(); }
class FileNode implements FsNode { private final long kb; FileNode(long kb) { this.kb = kb; } public long size() { return kb; } }
class FolderNode implements FsNode {
    private final List<FsNode> children = new ArrayList<>();
    FolderNode add(FsNode n) { children.add(n); return this; }
    public long size() { long s = 0; for (FsNode c : children) s += c.size(); return s; }
}
interface FsNode { fun size(): Long }
class FileNode(private val kb: Long) : FsNode { override fun size() = kb }
class FolderNode(private val children: MutableList<FsNode> = mutableListOf()) : FsNode {
    fun add(n: FsNode) = apply { children += n }
    override fun size() = children.sumOf { it.size() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Branching on instanceof in the client, which defeats the pattern.
  • Forgetting cycles: adding a folder inside itself loops forever.
  • Calling any list of objects a Composite; it needs the shared interface and recursion.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does add() go? -> Either on Component (uniform, leaves throw) or only on Composite (safe, clients cast).
  2. Cost of size() on a million files? -> O(n) per call unless cached and invalidated.
  3. Can a node have two parents? -> Then it is a graph, not a tree; Composite assumptions break (double counting).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines it with the file example. Senior adds transparency vs safety, cycle and depth risks, and caching invalidation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A permissions tree computed access by walking all ancestors with instanceof checks in 6 services; moving to a Composite interface removed the copies.

questions.contextHtml:
A file manager lets users drag folders. After a user dragged "Projects" into its own subfolder "Projects/2024", the app freezes and then logs:

java.lang.StackOverflowError
  at FolderNode.size(FolderNode.java:9)
  at FolderNode.size(FolderNode.java:9)
  ... (1024 more)
class FolderNode implements FsNode {
    private final List<FsNode> children = new ArrayList<>();
    FolderNode add(FsNode n) { children.add(n); return this; }
    public long size() { long s = 0; for (FsNode c : children) s += c.size(); return s; }
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the stack size." That only delays the crash and the tree is invalid anyway.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can nodes have multiple parents (shortcuts)? Is the tree mutated concurrently? Who calls add?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reject the move in the UI so no cycle can be created; repair the damaged data by detaching the node.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a cycle created by add; (b) a very deep but valid tree; (c) a bug in size caching. The repeated identical frame at line 9 points to a cycle.
  4. How I'd verify each: Walk parent pointers from the target upward; if the moved node is found, it is a cycle. Count depth on the real data to rule out (b).
  5. Root cause: add never validates that the new child is not an ancestor of (or equal to) the parent.
  6. Fix: Keep a parent reference; in add, walk up from this and throw if n is found.
  7. Prevention: a unit test that adds a folder to itself and to its descendant; model "move" as one validated operation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch StackOverflowError; the walk-up check costs O(depth) per add, which is trivial.
FolderNode add(FsNode n) {
    for (FolderNode p = this; p != null; p = p.parent)
        if (p == n) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cycle");
    if (n instanceof FolderNode f) f.parent = this;
    children.add(n);
    return this;
}
fun add(n: FsNode): FolderNode {
    var p: FolderNode? = this
    while (p != null) { require(p !== n) { "cycle" }; p = p.parent }
    (n as? FolderNode)?.parent = this
    children += n
    return this
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Symlinks make cycles legitimate. -> Then it is a graph: track a visited set during traversal.
  • Moving a node to a different parent? -> Remove from the old parent first, then validate and add.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a category tree in an admin tool accepted a parent change that made a loop; the storefront menu rendering took the site down until the row was fixed by hand.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises the stack size.
  • Hire: finds the cycle and validates in add.
  • Strong hire: adds parent pointers, validated move, tests, and addresses graphs with a visited set.

questions.promptHtml: Should add() and remove() live on the Component interface or only on the Composite? Argue both sides and say what you would pick.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the classic Composite API decision; it shows how you weigh uniformity against type safety.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Transparent puts add/remove on the interface so clients treat everything uniformly, but leaves must throw UnsupportedOperationException, a runtime failure. Safe puts them only on the composite, so the compiler protects you, but clients that build trees need the concrete type. I pick safe for most code, because mutation is usually done by a builder that knows it has a composite, while readers only need the shared interface.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Transparent follows GoF "uniformity": one type, no casts. Cost: a leaf violates Liskov (promises add but throws). Safe keeps the interface honest. Many designs use a third route: immutable composites built by a builder, so there is no add at all after construction, and the read operations remain uniform.

Transparent: Component{size, add, remove}  Leaf.add -> throws
Safe       : Component{size}               Folder{add, remove}

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface FsNode { long size(); }                       // safe: read-only contract
class FolderNode implements FsNode { FolderNode add(FsNode n) { /* ... */ return this; } /* size */ }
sealed interface FsNode { fun size(): Long }
class FolderNode(val children: List<FsNode>) : FsNode {   // immutable composite
    override fun size() = children.sumOf { it.size() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Transparent with silent no-op add on a leaf (hides bugs).
  • Safe design where clients cast everywhere.
  • Ignoring the immutable option.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which is Android View? -> ViewGroup has addView, View does not: safe style.
  2. LSP angle? -> Transparent leaves break it.
  3. Thread safety? -> Immutable composites are safe to share; mutable ones need external locking.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "GoF prefers transparency". Senior frames it as an LSP trade-off and proposes immutability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A widget toolkit with transparent addChild crashed in about 1 of 200 QA flows when a button received addChild; a separate Container type fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
An HR service computes cost for a manager hierarchy:

double cost(Object e) {
    if (e instanceof Developer d) return d.salary;
    if (e instanceof Designer d) return d.salary + d.toolsBudget;
    if (e instanceof Manager m) {
        double sum = m.salary;
        for (Object r : m.reports) sum += cost(r);
        return sum;
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();
}

There are 4 other methods (headcount, report, export...) each with the same instanceof ladder. Adding "Contractor" needed edits in 5 places and one was missed, giving a wrong headcount in a board report.
questions.promptHtml: Refactor to remove the ladders, and say which pattern and why.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a type enum and a switch; the same ladders just get a new shape.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it a strict tree? Do contractors cost differently? Will more operations or more node types be added more often?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the missed headcount branch now and add a test with one of each type.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The structure is part-whole with uniform operations: Composite fits. If operations multiplied and node types were stable, Visitor would be an alternative.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count change reasons in git history: new node types (Composite wins) versus new operations (Visitor wins).
  5. Root cause: Behavior sits outside the types, so every new type touches every operation.
  6. Fix: interface Staff { double cost(); int headcount(); }, Developer, Designer, Contractor as leaves, Manager as composite summing reports. Adding Contractor is one class.
  7. Prevention: a test with a tree containing every type, asserting every method; compile-time guarantee comes from the interface.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The interface gains an operation every time a report is added. For many unrelated operations I would use Visitor instead of bloating the interface.
interface Staff { double cost(); int headcount(); }
class Developer implements Staff { double salary; public double cost() { return salary; } public int headcount() { return 1; } }
class Manager implements Staff {
    double salary; List<Staff> reports = new ArrayList<>();
    public double cost() { return salary + reports.stream().mapToDouble(Staff::cost).sum(); }
    public int headcount() { return 1 + reports.stream().mapToInt(Staff::headcount).sum(); }
}
interface Staff { fun cost(): Double; fun headcount(): Int }
class Developer(private val salary: Double) : Staff { override fun cost() = salary; override fun headcount() = 1 }
class Manager(private val salary: Double, private val reports: List<Staff>) : Staff {
    override fun cost() = salary + reports.sumOf { it.cost() }
    override fun headcount() = 1 + reports.sumOf { it.headcount() }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 15 new reports are requested. -> The interface bloats; move to Visitor or external functions over a sealed hierarchy (Kotlin when is exhaustive).
  • Contractors report to two managers. -> Not a tree; double counting; model assignments separately.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a missed branch in one of five ladders under-reported headcount by 12 for a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: enum plus switch.
  • Hire: Composite with polymorphic methods.
  • Strong hire: also weighs Visitor by direction of change and flags the non-tree case.

questions.promptHtml: What does the Decorator pattern give you that subclassing does not? Use BufferedReader as the example.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you understand runtime composition and the combinatorial explosion that decorators avoid.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps, holds it, and adds behavior before or after delegating. Because layers are chosen at runtime and are stackable, I get n independent features with n classes. Subclassing needs a class per combination, up to 2^n, and fixes the choice at compile time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f))): the file stream is the component; InputStreamReader is an Adapter, BufferedReader a Decorator. Reading a file at 1 byte per call is 8,192 syscalls per 8 KB; a buffer cuts that to 1. Each wrapper overrides the methods it changes and forwards the rest.

Caller -> Buffering -> Encryption -> Compression -> FileSource

Order is behavior: compress-then-encrypt is not encrypt-then-compress (encrypted bytes do not compress).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

abstract class SourceDecorator implements Source {
    protected final Source inner;
    SourceDecorator(Source inner) { this.inner = inner; }
}
class UpperCase extends SourceDecorator {
    UpperCase(Source s) { super(s); }
    public String read() { return inner.read().toUpperCase(); }
}
class UpperCase(private val inner: Source) : Source by inner {
    override fun read() = inner.read().uppercase()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the wrapper must implement the same interface.
  • Assuming order does not matter.
  • Identity checks (==, instanceof) failing on wrappers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Decorator vs Proxy? -> Same shape; Decorator adds behavior, Proxy controls access.
  2. Why is Java verbose here? -> Every interface method must be forwarded; Kotlin by generates it.
  3. Where does Decorator hurt? -> Huge interfaces and deep stacks that are hard to debug.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "adds responsibilities dynamically". Senior gives the 2^n vs n count, order sensitivity and the Kotlin by shortcut.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Stacked wrappers around an HTTP client with logging after retry doubled log volume by about 40 GB/day; the fix was reordering.

questions.contextHtml: A coffee app prices drinks with subclasses: Espresso, EspressoWithMilk, EspressoWithMilkAndCaramel, LatteWithCaramel, and so on: 23 classes today. Marketing wants an oat-milk option, a "double shot", and a 10% happy-hour discount that stacks with any add-ons but never applies to the loyalty reward drink. Two new add-ons a month are expected.
questions.promptHtml: Redesign it. Which classes change when a new add-on arrives, and where does the discount go?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds boolean flags (hasMilk, hasCaramel) to one class with a giant price() full of ifs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do add-ons change description and price only, or also preparation steps? Does the discount apply to the total or to specific items? Are add-ons ordered in any way?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; freeze new subclasses.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Decorator for add-ons (stackable, independent); discount might be a decorator applied last, or a pricing rule outside the drink.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check combinations: with 6 add-ons subclassing would need up to 2^6 = 64 variants; decorators need 6.
  5. Root cause: Features modelled as subclasses.
  6. Fix: interface Drink { String desc(); double price(); }; Espresso, Latte as bases; Milk, OatMilk, Caramel, DoubleShot as decorators; HappyHour decorator that applies 10% to the inner price and is added last. A new add-on is one new class and zero edits to existing ones (open/closed). The reward drink is built without the HappyHour layer.
  7. Prevention: tests on price for representative stacks, including the discount order (discount applied to the full inner price, not before add-ons).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: If the discount rules grow (coupons, tiers), I would move them to a pricing service on the order, not stack discount decorators.
interface Drink { String desc(); double price(); }
class Espresso implements Drink { public String desc() { return "espresso"; } public double price() { return 100; } }
abstract class AddOn implements Drink {
    protected final Drink inner;
    AddOn(Drink d) { inner = d; }
}
class OatMilk extends AddOn {
    OatMilk(Drink d) { super(d); }
    public String desc() { return inner.desc() + "+oat"; }
    public double price() { return inner.price() + 40; }
}
class HappyHour extends AddOn {
    HappyHour(Drink d) { super(d); }
    public String desc() { return inner.desc() + " (happy hour)"; }
    public double price() { return inner.price() * 0.9; }
}
interface Drink { fun desc(): String; fun price(): Double }
class OatMilk(private val inner: Drink) : Drink by inner {
    override fun desc() = inner.desc() + "+oat"
    override fun price() = inner.price() + 40
}
class HappyHour(private val inner: Drink) : Drink by inner {
    override fun price() = inner.price() * 0.9
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Discount must apply only to add-ons, not the base drink. -> Then it is not a pure wrapper; give add-ons a price component or move the rule to pricing.
  • Need to find whether a drink has oat milk. -> Do not instanceof-hunt through wrappers; expose an add-on list or compute it in a domain object.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a menu system with 60 subclasses needed a release for each new topping; after moving to decorators, marketing configured new ones from a catalog.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flags and ifs.
  • Hire: decorators, new add-on is one class, discount as outermost layer.
  • Strong hire: gives class-count math, discusses order and when pricing rules should leave the decorator chain.

questions.contextHtml:
A backup tool writes archives to disk. A new "secure backup" feature wraps the writer. Archive size went from about 12 MB to about 100 MB per 100 MB of data, and backups got slower by 4x, though the compression flag is on.

Sink sink = new FileSink(path);
sink = new CompressingSink(sink);     // gzip
sink = new EncryptingSink(sink);      // AES
sink.write(data);

The data flows: caller -> EncryptingSink -> CompressingSink -> FileSink.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what is the correct stack? Anything else you would check?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compression is probably not working; check the gzip level."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which direction does write flow through the layers? Is the restore path symmetrical? Are keys/IV random per file?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Backups are valid, only bloated; swap the order and keep a note for old archives.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) encrypt-then-compress, so gzip sees random-looking bytes; (b) gzip level misconfigured; (c) disk slow.
  4. How I'd verify each: Gzip a sample of the ciphertext with gzip -c and compare size to the plaintext (about 100% vs about 12%); check call order in a debugger.
  5. Root cause: The outermost decorator is called first, so the data was encrypted before it reached the compressor. Ciphertext has no redundancy.
  6. Fix: Data must be compressed first and encrypted second. The outermost decorator runs first, so compression must be the outer layer and encryption the inner one: new CompressingSink(new EncryptingSink(new FileSink(path))).
  7. Prevention: a unit test asserting the compressed size of a repetitive input is below 20%; document layer order in the factory and test the restore round trip.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Compress-then-encrypt can leak length information in some protocols (compression oracle attacks such as CRIME/BREACH on attacker-influenced data); for file archives it is the usual choice, but I would verify the threat model.
Sink sink = new CompressingSink(new EncryptingSink(new FileSink(path)));
val sink: Sink = CompressingSink(EncryptingSink(FileSink(path)))

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Restore order? -> Reverse it: decrypt, then decompress.
  • How do you stop future mistakes? -> Hide the order inside a SinkFactory.secureBackup(path).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a nightly job with encrypt-then-compress ran for months with 8x storage cost; a reviewer noticed because the "compressed" files had a flat entropy profile.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes gzip.
  • Hire: finds the inverted order and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: tests the ratio, hides order in a factory, notes the security nuance of compress-then-encrypt.

questions.contextHtml:
An HttpClient interface has 28 methods. A team built 9 decorators around it: auth, retry, logging, metrics, tracing, cache, circuit breaker, timeout, redirect. Log volume tripled to about 120 GB/day after a refactor, p99 rose from 180 ms to 260 ms, and a stack trace is 40 frames deep:

at LoggingClient.get(LoggingClient.java:31)
at RetryingClient.get(RetryingClient.java:44)
at LoggingClient.get(LoggingClient.java:31)   <- second logging layer
at MetricsClient.get(...)
... 36 more wrapper frames

Each decorator forwards all 28 methods by hand; 5 of them forgot to forward close(), and file descriptors leak slowly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove two decorators." That ignores the structural problems: forwarding boilerplate, order dependence and no tests.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which wrappers do all 28 methods need? Where is the stack assembled? Who changed the assembly recently?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the duplicated logging layer (log volume) and add close() forwarding in the five wrappers (leak).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) logging inserted twice by the refactor; (b) retry wrapping logging, so each attempt logs; (c) per-layer overhead (small, about microseconds), unlikely the whole 80 ms; (d) a retry storm adds latency.
  4. How I'd verify each: Dump the assembled chain at startup (toString of each layer); compare logs per request ID; check retry counters and lsof | wc -l growth for descriptors.
  5. Root cause: An undocumented, untested order plus manual forwarding on a fat interface. The tripled logs come from duplicate and retried logging.
  6. Fix: Short-term fix the order and forward close(). Long-term: Kotlin by delegation or a dynamic proxy removes forwarding; better, replace the hand-built stack with an interceptor chain (OkHttp-style) where each step handles one request and proceed, built once by a single factory with a test that pins the order.
  7. Prevention: an assembly test that asserts the layer order; interface segregation (a client with 4 operations, not 28).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not drop retry or tracing; they are needed. Interceptors reduce boilerplate but make domain logic invisible if misused, so keep them for cross-cutting concerns.
class LoggingClient(private val inner: HttpClient) : HttpClient by inner {   // forwards all 28 incl. close()
    override fun get(url: String): Response = inner.get(url).also { log(url, it.code) }
}
// Java: forward only what changes by extending a base that delegates everything
abstract class ForwardingClient implements HttpClient {
    protected final HttpClient inner;
    ForwardingClient(HttpClient c) { inner = c; }
    public Response get(String url) { return inner.get(url); }
    public void close() { inner.close(); }
    // ... remaining methods once, here
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would AOP be better? -> It removes boilerplate but hides order in annotations; use only if the team knows the proxy rules (self-invocation).
  • Retry must be inside circuit breaker or outside? -> Usually breaker outermost counting final failures, with retry inside; decide and test.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a duplicated logging layer doubled the cost of the log pipeline for a week before a cost alert fired.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: removes wrappers at random.
  • Hire: finds duplicate logging, forwarding bug, proposes a single assembly.
  • Strong hire: segregates the interface, uses delegation or chains, pins order in a test.

questions.contextHtml: You wrote RateLimitingSender (max 2 messages per user), LoggingSender and TwilioAdapter as decorators of Sender. The team asks how to test without hitting Twilio, what to assert about the rate limiter, and how to prove that a blocked message is not logged or sent.
questions.promptHtml: Describe the tests (unit per decorator and one for the assembled chain) and show the key one.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: One big integration test calling real Twilio, or mocking everything and asserting nothing about order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the clock part of the limit (per minute)? Is it shared across servers? Should blocked sends return false or throw?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; this is test design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: What can break: each decorator's own logic; the order; resource forwarding.
  4. How I'd verify each: Use a recording fake Sender as the inner object; for the limiter, send 3 and assert the fake saw 2 and the third returned false; for logging, assert one log per forwarded call using a captured appender; for the chain, assert with the fake at the bottom that a blocked call never reaches it.
  5. Root cause: N/A.
  6. Fix: Because decorators take the inner object by constructor, every layer is testable alone with a fake; the assembled test pins the order.
  7. Prevention: a time source injected into the limiter for deterministic tests; a chain-assembly test in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a real clock sleep in tests, and I would not test the vendor SDK through the decorators; the adapter gets its own test.
class RecordingSender implements Sender {
    final List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>();
    public boolean send(String u, String t) { sent.add(u + ":" + t); return true; }
}
void blockedMessageNeverReachesInner() {
    RecordingSender fake = new RecordingSender();
    Sender s = new RateLimitingSender(new LoggingSender(fake), 2);
    s.send("u", "1"); s.send("u", "2");
    assert !s.send("u", "3");
    assert fake.sent.size() == 2;
}
class RecordingSender : Sender {
    val sent = mutableListOf<String>()
    override fun send(user: String, text: String): Boolean { sent += "$user:$text"; return true }
}
// RateLimitingSender(LoggingSender(fake), 2): third send returns false and fake.sent.size == 2

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Limit is per minute. -> Inject a Clock; advance a fake clock in the test.
  • Multi-server limits? -> The in-memory map is wrong; use a shared counter (for example Redis with a TTL) and integration-test it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a limiter placed after the vendor call passed every unit test but cost money on blocked sends; only an order-pinning test would have caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: live vendor test.
  • Hire: fake inner per decorator, plus blocked-call assertion.
  • Strong hire: injected clock, order test for the assembled chain, separate adapter test.

questions.promptHtml: Decorator and Composite both have "a wrapper with the same interface as what it holds". How do they differ, and when would you combine them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It probes whether you reason by arity and intent instead of by UML shape.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Composite holds many children of the same type and aggregates their results to model a part-whole tree. Decorator holds exactly one inner and adds behavior to it. A decorator is like a composite with one child whose job is to add something, not to aggregate. I combine them to decorate a node anywhere in a tree, such as adding a border to any View, leaf or group.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Composite Decorator Inheritance
Holds many same-type children one inner n/a
Goal uniform part-whole add behavior specialize at compile time
Runtime change add/remove children stack/unstack no

A scroll bar added with ScrollDecorator(textBox) is a Decorator; a window containing widgets is a Composite. Combined: ScrollDecorator(new Panel(children...)) works because both implement Widget.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface Widget { void draw(); }
class Panel implements Widget { List<Widget> kids = new ArrayList<>(); public void draw() { kids.forEach(Widget::draw); } }
class Border implements Widget {
    private final Widget inner;
    Border(Widget w) { inner = w; }
    public void draw() { System.out.println("border"); inner.draw(); }
}
interface Widget { fun draw() }
class Panel(private val kids: List<Widget>) : Widget { override fun draw() = kids.forEach { it.draw() } }
class Border(private val inner: Widget) : Widget by inner { override fun draw() { println("border"); inner.draw() } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Decorator is just inheritance"; it is runtime and stackable.
  • Confusing "has many" with "wraps one".
  • Forgetting that decorating a composite wraps the whole subtree, not each child.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Real Android examples? -> ViewGroup is Composite, ContextWrapper is Decorator.
  2. Does a decorator of a composite expose add()? -> Not through the base interface; keep a reference to the panel.
  3. Proxy difference? -> Proxy controls access to its subject; Decorator adds behavior.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives definitions. Senior explains arity, intent, and the combination pattern with its pitfalls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A UI library decorating widgets with analytics wrappers lost clicks because getChildAt returned the wrapper instead of the real widget.

questions.contextHtml:
A cloud storage dashboard shows "folder size" using a Composite: size() recurses over the tree. It worked with 10,000 files. A customer now has 8 million files in a tree 400 levels deep (generated paths). Dashboard requests for the root folder take 14 s, CPU is pegged, and a few requests die with StackOverflowError. The page is requested every 5 s per open dashboard and there are 300 open dashboards.

GET /folders/root/size  p50=11.2s p99=14.8s  60 rps, 5xx=3%
jstack: 40 threads in FolderNode.size (deep recursion)
questions.promptHtml: What do you change in the model and the code?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a cache with 5 minutes TTL" without noticing that the O(n) walk per update and the stack depth remain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How fresh must sizes be? How often do files change? Are totals needed for every folder or only at the root and on demand?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Serve the last computed value with a staleness label, limit recomputation to one in flight per folder, and cap request rate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) O(n) recursion per request: 8M nodes x 60 rps is far too much; (b) deep recursion causing stack overflow; (c) GC pressure from boxed iterators.
  4. How I'd verify each: Profile with a flame graph; check node count and max depth; count recomputations per minute.
  5. Root cause: The Composite recursion is a fine model but a bad execution strategy at this size; recomputing a pure aggregate on every read.
  6. Fix: Keep the interface, change the implementation: store an aggregate sizeBytes per folder and update it incrementally on file add/remove by walking up the ancestors (O(depth) per write), or compute asynchronously and store. Use an iterative traversal with an explicit stack for any full walk, so depth does not matter.
  7. Prevention: load tests with deep and wide synthetic trees; alert on size latency.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Incremental totals risk drift if an update is missed; schedule a periodic reconciliation. I would not raise -Xss.
long sizeIterative(FsNode root) {
    Deque<FsNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(root); long total = 0;
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        FsNode n = stack.pop();
        if (n instanceof FolderNode f) f.children().forEach(stack::push); else total += n.ownSize();
    }
    return total;
}
fun sizeIterative(root: FsNode): Long {
    val stack = ArrayDeque<FsNode>().apply { add(root) }
    var total = 0L
    while (stack.isNotEmpty()) {
        when (val n = stack.removeLast()) {
            is FolderNode -> stack.addAll(n.children)
            else -> total += n.ownSize()
        }
    }
    return total
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Files change 1,000 times per second under the root. -> Incremental updates hit the root's hot counter; batch updates or accept eventual totals.
  • Is Composite wrong here? -> No; the model stays, the aggregate is materialized.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a size dashboard that was fine in the pilot took down a storage API when one customer imported a deep tree; caching per folder with incremental updates fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: TTL cache and bigger stack.
  • Hire: materialized aggregates and iterative traversal.
  • Strong hire: discusses incremental update drift, hot-root contention, reconciliation and the staleness contract.

questions.contextHtml:
A service keeps active sessions in List<String> sessions = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()) because "it is thread-safe". Under load (about 50 threads) the logs show:

java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
  at java.util.ArrayList$Itr.next
  at SessionReaper.cleanup(SessionReaper.java:27)

and duplicates appear in the list although the code checks first:

if (!sessions.contains(id)) sessions.add(id);      // check-then-act
for (String s : sessions) { if (expired(s)) sessions.remove(s); }   // reaper
questions.promptHtml: synchronizedList is a Decorator. Explain what it guarantees, why these bugs happen, and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap more things in synchronizedList" or "add synchronized to the reaper method".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is order needed? Are lookups frequent? How big is the list? Is expiry time-based?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Wrap check-then-add in synchronized (sessions); make the reaper iterate over a snapshot or use removeIf.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) iteration is not atomic; the decorator locks each call, not the loop; (b) check-then-act spans two locked calls; (c) removing from a list while iterating it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run a stress test with 50 threads adding the same id and assert uniqueness; the CME stack points to the iterator, which confirms (a)/(c).
  5. Root cause: The decorator adds per-method locking only. Compound operations and iteration are outside its guarantee (the Javadoc requires manual synchronization on the list during iteration).
  6. Fix: Use a data structure matching the need: ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() with add (atomic, returns false if present) and removeIf; or ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> with expiry timestamps.
  7. Prevention: review rule: "synchronizedX" wrappers are not enough for compound actions; stress test in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A single synchronized block around everything works but serializes the hot path; I would use concurrent structures.
Set<String> sessions = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
sessions.add(id);                       // atomic: no duplicates
sessions.removeIf(this::expired);       // safe weakly consistent traversal
val sessions: MutableSet<String> = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()
sessions.add(id)
sessions.removeIf { expired(it) }

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Order of insertion matters. -> ConcurrentLinkedQueue or a lock-protected LinkedHashSet; decide the consistency you need.
  • Why not CopyOnWriteArrayList? -> Fine for read-mostly small lists; every write copies the array (O(n)), bad for 100k sessions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "thread-safe" wrapped map still produced double charges because a read-then-write sequence was not atomic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more synchronized wrappers.
  • Hire: knows per-call locking vs compound actions and fixes with a concurrent set.
  • Strong hire: also reasons about ordering needs, copy-on-write cost and a stress test.
